concepts.title: Social Change: Types, Causes and the Role of Resistance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Social Change: Types, Causes and the Role of Resistance' refers to.
questions.a: Social change is the transformation over time of institutions, relationships and patterns of living. It arrives through many doors -- technology, economy, environment, ideas and social movements -- and it always meets friction, for established interests and habits resist rearrangement. Change is uneven: some domains race ahead while others lag.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Social Change: Types, Causes and the Role of Resistance'.
questions.a: Nothing social stands still -- but change travels unevenly and always drags resistance behind it.

concepts.title: Social Order: The Made Regularity of Social Life

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Social Order: The Made Regularity of Social Life' refers to.
questions.a: Social order is the patterned predictability of social life -- the fact that traffic flows, queues hold and offices run. Sociologists stress it is an accomplishment, not a natural state: it is produced and maintained by authority, accepted rules and often by coercion, and it can break down in revolution, war or crisis.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Social Order: The Made Regularity of Social Life'.
questions.a: Order is not the absence of change but its management -- made, kept, and breakable.

concepts.title: Village, Town and City: Rural and Urban Life Compared

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Village, Town and City: Rural and Urban Life Compared' refers to.
questions.a: Rural society is marked by small scale, proximity and dense face-to-face ties -- everyone knows everyone, and agriculture anchors life. Urban society is larger, denser and more heterogeneous, specialised and anonymous, with formal rules filling the gaps that intimacy fills in villages. Each also changes the other through migration, media and markets.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Village, Town and City: Rural and Urban Life Compared'.
questions.a: Village life runs on familiarity, city life on anonymity and rules -- two social worlds in continuous exchange.

concepts.title: Ecology of the City and Rural Change

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Ecology of the City and Rural Change' refers to.
questions.a: Cities are built environments where geography, economy and planning interact: land use sorts into commercial, industrial and residential zones, shaped by transport and profit. Villages too are changing -- new crops, roads, schooling and communications dissolve the timeless-village image, making both rural and urban worlds works in progress.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Ecology of the City and Rural Change'.
questions.a: The city is a planned-and-sprawl ecology; the village is no museum -- both are mid-change landscapes.
